title: Drug culture, squares and how critics saw the new music
summary: Discussion of musicians splitting by drug habits and whether boppers respected older players.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Yeah, we were talking about this before too the way this separated people because those who were smoking were, cir you know, those who were drinking and then those who were using heroin.
Yeah.
If you didn't use it, you were considered a square you know, they didn't want you to be a part of that.
Yeah.

And as I brought up, I think that had a lot to do with the way certain people looked at the music, some of the critics, because if they couldn't relate socially to the musicians as they always had, then it stopped them from evaluating the music in a proper way.
I think that's fair enough. By the same token it was a fair analysis as to fellow musicians.
Yeah.
Because the difference between square music
and being on the ball and all that sort of stuff. I think they lost a lot of the heritage of what they were doing.
Well yet they always had to respect the giants of the previous era.
They didn't.
You don't think so?
No.
You don't think they respected Hawk and Ben and Prez?
No.
Oh, I always felt that they did.
No.
They always put down Dixielanders, but they always spoke with reverence for these kind of people.
Well, not reverence reverence.
Respect certainly. I never heard them really put down their music. Not the real players, you know.
Well, you call names there, you called Hawks and off Prez and --
Yeah.
But then you had Coltrane.
Well, that came much later. We are talking about, you know, when bebop first came into --
